texts.facts: These revision petitions were filed by accused Nos.2 and 3 in S.T.No. 181 of 2000 on the files of the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Kozhikode. The second accused was convicted and sentenced by the courts below under Section 16 (1)(a) (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act,1954 read with Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules,1955 and the third accused was convicted and sentenced by the courts below under Section 16 (1) (a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. 2. Heard. 3. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 27.7.1998, PW1, the Food Inspector purchased two packets of curd from the first accused. The second accused was the owner of the shop and the third accused was the Crl.R.P.Nos. 2371 & 2571 of 2006 manufacturer. After sampling as per rules, one of the samples was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis. The Public Analyst filed Ext.P12 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for the food item and was therefore adulterated. Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext.P20 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would also show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for the food item and was therefore adulterated. It was further alleged that the second accused did not have the licence under the PFA Rules to sell the food item. Ali Mansoor Kodakkadan vs The Food Inspector on 8 February, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73255914/ 2 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW6 were examined and Exts.P1 to P31 series were marked for the prosecution. DW1 was examined and Ext.D1 was marked for the revision petitioners.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the Crl.R.P.Nos. 2371 & 2571 of 2006 food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P20 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. 6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act. Therefore, Ext.P20 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra). It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not Crl.R.P.Nos. 2371 & 2571 of 2006 admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
